name: Elena Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Elena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run blast-hole drills at Granite Flats, an open-pit iron ore mine. The drill makes the holes the explosives go into, so if my pattern's off, the whole blast is off. Three days a week I'm out in the pit in the cab, and two days I'm in the remote centre in town, watching three drills that mostly run themselves and stepping in when one hits bad ground. I like the puzzle of it. What wears me out is the drive and the noise, and the meetings about meetings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you find the remote days compared with the pit?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, I like them more than I expected. I use an AI assistant every day now, for writing up shift reports, for reading the drill data, even for figuring out what's for dinner. Some of the older drillers think I'm a traitor for liking it. My mate Hugh calls the remote centre the fish tank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a bit of a letdown. At work I'd joke that I'll still be driving out to the pit when I'm sixty. Online I'd probably post something about how the money should go into safety and training instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be a bit disappointed. I've been learning this stuff because I think it's where things are going, and I like it. If it stalls, I've just got a nice skill that makes my reports quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am, using the AI tools every day because they already save me an hour a shift. I'd keep my two remote days and keep putting money into the index fund each month. Sam and I would carry on with the café plans, nothing changes there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little bored maybe. Like being all dressed up and the party's cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be disappointed. Isn't that an unusual thing for a miner to say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. Hugh would say so. But I've done twenty years of shaking in a cab, and my back's not what it was. The remote centre is the first time I've thought I could do this job until I'm sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do Sam and the kids make of you liking the AI stuff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam rolls his eyes. Ruby and Finn are ten and think it's normal, they ask it about volcanoes. The café is the bit Sam cares about, and I've helped him with the ordering using the same tools.

S0.say: I'd say it's a bit of a letdown and joke that I'll be driving out to the pit when I'm sixty. Online I'd post that the money should go into safety and training instead.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed, because I've been learning this stuff and I like it. If it stalls, I've just got a handy skill that makes my reports quicker.
S0.do: Keeps using AI tools daily because they save her an hour a shift, and keeps her two remote days. Keeps adding to her index fund every month and supports her partner's café plans.
S0.feel: Calm, slightly bored and a little let down.
S0.quote: Like being all dressed up and the party's cancelled.
S0.fieldNote: Elena is the rare miner who'd be disappointed by a stall in AI, mainly because remote work spares her back. She's frank that colleagues see her as a traitor for liking it. Her progressive streak shows up in where she wants the money to go rather than in fear for her job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment the union has to bargain hard, not just say no. We want training paid for, remote jobs offered to the people already here, and a slice of the savings. I'd post that and I'd say it loud in the fish tank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm one of the lucky ones, and that makes me uncomfortable. I'm already in the remote centre, and I'm good with the tools. Hugh isn't, and he's got the same kids and the same mortgage as me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the automation technician course the company runs, so I'm not just watching drills but fixing their programming. I'd volunteer to train other drillers on the remote system, Hugh first if he'd let me. And I'd go to the union meetings and push for a profit-sharing deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a bit of guilt mixed in. It's strange to feel safe when your friends don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to Hugh?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy him a coffee at Sam's café and say, mate, give me two afternoons and I'll show you the system. He'd grumble. But he'd come, because he's not stupid, just proud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you want a slice of the savings. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not an accountant. But if one remote operator replaces three drillers, the company saves two wages. I'd want some of that in a training fund and some in our pay. Otherwise it's all going to shareholders who've never been in a pit.

S1.say: I'd say this is when the union must bargain hard rather than just say no. We want paid training, remote jobs offered to people already here, and a slice of the savings.
S1.think: I think I'm one of the lucky ones, which makes me uncomfortable. I'm already in the remote centre and good with the tools, and colleagues like Hugh aren't.
S1.do: Enrols in the company's automation technician course and volunteers to train other drillers on the remote system. Pushes the union for a profit-sharing deal on the wage savings.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, mixed with guilt about feeling safe while friends don't.
S1.quote: He'd come, because he's not stupid, just proud.
S1.fieldNote: Elena's adaptability puts her ahead, and her politics make her uneasy about it. She wants the union to bargain over the gains rather than block the change. Her plan to teach Hugh herself is a small, personal version of the policy she wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly the thing we've been warning about: the companies get a fortune overnight and nobody's ready. I'd push for an emergency fund, paid for by taxing the profits from automation. I'd go to rallies with the twins in tow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think even my remote job goes. If AI can do almost anything, it doesn't need me watching three drills, it watches three hundred. All my early learning buys me months, not years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move more money into savings straight away and stop putting into the index fund for a bit, though I might buy some shares in the automation companies, grimly, if that's where all the money's going. I'd help organise the union to demand the emergency fund. And I'd sit down with Sam about whether the café can carry us for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, we've got savings and the café, but it's the first time I've felt clever learning won't save me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying shares in the automation companies sounds like it might clash with your politics. Does it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Completely. I'd hate it. But if they're the ones getting the money, I'd rather some of it came back to my kids than none. I'd still vote to tax them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning give you, in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very little. I'd try to get the automation tech ticket finished, but two years is about the length of the course. I'd come out of it right as the job disappears. It's like training for a race that's already been won.

S2.say: I'd say this is what we've warned about: companies get a fortune overnight and nobody's ready. I'd push for an emergency fund paid by taxing automation profits, and I'd go to rallies with the twins.
S2.think: I think even my remote job goes, because an AI can watch three hundred drills, not three. All my early learning buys me months, not years.
S2.do: Moves money into savings and pauses her index fund, while grudgingly buying some shares in automation companies. Helps the union campaign for an emergency fund and works out with her partner whether the café can carry the family.
S2.feel: Anxious; savings keep her from panic, but she feels for the first time that learning won't save her.
S2.quote: It's like training for a race that's already been won.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI is the one picture where Elena's early learning stops helping, and she says so without flinching. She names the clash between her politics and buying automation shares and holds both. The café, previously a side interest, becomes part of the family's safety plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but long enough to fight for the right deal. I'd be campaigning for profit-sharing laws and free retraining. I'd say it at work, and I'd probably stand for something in the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is tricky. I'd finish the automation course and get maybe three years of work out of it. After that I don't know, and I'd be forty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the automation tech course in the first eighteen months. I'd keep investing every month and add to it, because if machines do the work, owning a bit of them matters. I'd also start learning how the café's numbers work properly, because a small business with people in it might be our next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see a few moves ahead, but not the end of the game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A head start that's actually worth something. Two years, I'd finish the course as the job vanished. Five, I'd get paid for what I learned before it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the twins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the world's changing faster than when I was their age, and it's okay. They should learn to fix and build things, and be good with people. Finn wants to be a chef like his dad, and I think a person cooking still counts for something.

S3.say: I'd say five years is short but long enough to fight for the right deal. I'd campaign for profit-sharing laws and free retraining, and probably stand for a union role.
S3.think: I'd finish the automation course and get maybe three years of work from it. After that I don't know, and I'd be 48.
S3.do: Finishes the automation technician course within eighteen months and keeps adding to her investments monthly. Starts learning the café's finances properly as a possible next step for the family.
S3.feel: Uneasy; she can see a few moves ahead but not the end.
S3.quote: Five, I'd get paid for what I learned before it goes.
S3.fieldNote: Elena treats the five-year picture as a short window to cash in on what she's learned. Her belief in owning a share of the machines grows steadily across the AGI scenarios. The café keeps edging from Sam's project to the household's fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to build something fair, so let's not waste it. I'd want profit-sharing written into law and free retraining for anyone, any age. I'd be at every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is a career. I could move into automation tech, work it for six or seven years, then move into something else. I'd be fifty-three, and the twins would be at university.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the automation course in the first year or two and look for a job in robotics maintenance, maybe at the remote centre. I'd keep investing. And I'd help Sam turn the café into something bigger, maybe a second shop, because people will still want somewhere to sit and talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. The end point is still strange, but I'd have time to steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the end point is strange. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even with ten years, the AI ends up doing nearly everything. I'd have a good run, but at fifty-three I'd still be asking what's left. I don't think anyone knows the answer, and I'm suspicious of people who say they do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hugh, still. Ten years means he can dig in for nine of them and then fall off a cliff. I'd keep nagging him, but I can't make him learn.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough time to build something fair. I'd want profit-sharing in law and free retraining for anyone at any age, and I'd be at every meeting.
S4.think: For me, ten years is a career: automation tech for six or seven years, then something else. I'd be 53 and the twins would be at university.
S4.do: Finishes the automation course within two years and looks for robotics maintenance work, possibly in the remote centre. Keeps investing and helps her partner plan a second café.
S4.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, with time to steer even if the end is unclear.
S4.quote: Ten years means he can dig in for nine of them and then fall off a cliff.
S4.fieldNote: Elena is clear that ten years helps her a lot without solving the bigger question of what's left when AI does nearly everything. She admits she doesn't know the answer. Her recurring worry for Hugh shows she sees the long warning period as a trap for people who resist change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because all the learning I've done gets wiped out before it pays off. What would help is a law that shares the profits from automation, through a fund or a tax, and paid retraining that's actually available to everyone. Not a website with courses nobody has time for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to like the thing that might replace you. I enjoy these tools, I'm good with them, and they're still coming for my job. That's a strange place to stand.

headlineQuote: I enjoy these tools, I'm good with them, and they're still coming for my job.
portrait: Elena Walsh is 43 and runs blast-hole drills at the Granite Flats iron ore mine, splitting her week between the pit and a remote control centre in town. She uses AI tools every day, enjoys them, and would be faintly disappointed if AI stalled. Her early learning keeps her calm through the gentler scenarios, but fast AGI leaves her anxious because no amount of learning keeps up. Her progressive politics show in a steady push for profit-sharing and retraining, and she grudgingly buys shares in the companies she wants taxed. Her partner's café slowly becomes the family's plan B.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because all her learning would be wiped out before it paid off.
whatWouldHelp: A law that shares automation profits through a fund or a tax, and paid retraining that's genuinely available to everyone.
